title: The ten-minute kitchen word walk: twelve bilingual words, no printer
description: A ten-minute bilingual vocabulary routine that uses the objects already on your counter. Twelve words, one room, nothing to print and nothing to buy.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: The ten-minute kitchen word walk: twelve bilingual words, no printer
body:
Most bilingual activity ideas start with a download. You find the worksheet, you realise the printer is out of ink, and the activity never happens. The kitchen fixes that: it is full of objects a child can touch, and touching is what makes a word stick.

Here is the routine. It takes ten minutes and you do it standing up.

Pick one shelf or one drawer. Not the whole kitchen — one shelf. Twelve objects is plenty for a session.

Walk along it with your child and name each object in the language you are building, then in the other one: "la cuchara — the spoon". Let them repeat only if they want to. Pressure is what ends these sessions early.

Go round a second time, but this time you say the word and they point. Pointing is easier than speaking, and it shows you what landed without turning the game into a test.

Third round, swap roles: they say a word, you point. Children correct adults with great enthusiasm, and a child correcting you is a child using the language.

Stop while it is still fun. Ten minutes, twelve words, done. If you stop at the first sign of boredom, tomorrow's session starts from a good memory.

The next day, use five of the same words in a real sentence during dinner: "pass me la cuchara, please". Recycling beats a new list. A word used at the table three days in a row does more than thirty words named once.

Two things to avoid. Do not translate every sentence you say all day — it teaches the child to wait for the translation. And do not keep score: a child who senses a test stops guessing, and guessing is how vocabulary grows.

If you want the themed lists ready-made — kitchen, bathroom, school bag, weather — with the activities written next to them, that is what a vocabulary book is for. You read it on a screen and copy the week's twelve words onto paper.
qa_checklist: A bilingual (EN/ES) reader checks both languages, not a tool
No claims about fluency, test scores or developmental outcomes
Every activity works with what is already in the house: no printer, no purchase
Original text written for this page, not lifted from the book
CTA is honest: a Kindle vocabulary book read on a screen, lists copied into a notebook
semantic_review: Written for an English-dominant parent raising a Spanish-learning child, which matches the book's English-first structure. Spanish fragments kept to single words inside English sentences.
flagged_uncertainty: 'la cuchara — the spoon' order assumes Spanish is the target language; half the book's buyers may be Spanish-dominant parents building English. A bilingual reviewer should confirm the framing or we publish a mirrored version.
claims_check: No outcome promises. The text says what to do and how long it takes; it does not claim fluency, school results or cognitive benefits.
